source.quote: SMSL's own product page for the D200, read 2026-11-24: « the use of a Roma BD34352EKV decoder chip, distortion as low as 0.00019%(-114dB) »; « USB, Optical, and Coaxial inputs support DSD, Optical and Coaxial inputs support DoP64 »; « USB using XMOS XU-316, a real 32bit USB program, support DoP and native DSD, PCM support up to 768kHz, DSD support to DSD512 »; « Qualcomm's new generation of Bluetooth chips, support for LDAC (24bit/96kHz) »; « Support for external clock inputs, standard 10MHz clock or atomic clock inputs ».

facts.chip: ROHM BD34352EKV as the converter - SMSL's page spells the vendor « Roma » in one sentence and « ROHM » in its own heading, which is a typo in the source and not two parts - with an XMOS XU-316 as the USB interface and a Qualcomm part for Bluetooth. Three roles again: converter, interface, wireless.

_dsd_per_input_from_one_sentence: « USB, Optical, and Coaxial inputs support DSD, Optical and Coaxial inputs support DoP64 » splits the transports exactly: all three take DSD, and the two S/PDIF ones take it as DoP64. So dop_possible is true on all three and native_dsd_possible only on USB, where the maker says « support DoP and native DSD ». NO PCM CEILING is recorded for optical or coaxial: the 768 kHz figure is stated in the USB sentence and nowhere else, so those two inputs carry a DSD transport and no rate - the first record here where an input block holds a transport flag without a ceiling, which is what per-input fields were registered for.
